title: Seniority Doesn't Give You Certainty
author: Andrea Chiarelli
source: The Art of Asking Questions (theartofaskingquestions.com), August 26, 2026
summary: Andrea Chiarelli, drawing on a conversation with leadership coach Colette Molteni, dismantles the illusion that senior leaders possess some special certainty junior staff lack. The piece argues that confident-looking snap decisions from above are usually the product of practice at tolerating discomfort, not superior knowledge. Molteni offers a practical diagnostic for telling genuine deliberation from decision-avoidance: watch whether real work happens between meetings, not just whether meetings keep happening. The conversation also tackles how much uncertainty a leader should visibly show a team, landing on language that names an unresolved variable honestly without transmitting panic. Chiarelli's closing line reframes seniority not as certainty but as familiarity with the feeling of not knowing.
points: Distinguishes genuinely open decisions from disguised avoidance using an observable test: whether tangible work (writing, building, deciding) happens between check-in meetings, not just whether meetings occur.
Offers embodied cues for reading whether someone is deliberating or stalling, since avoidance and genuine wrestling can look identical from outside a decision.
Reframes emotional transparency in leadership: naming a specific unresolved variable is honest without being contagious, whereas voicing raw panic destabilizes the team.
Undercuts the myth of executive certainty by showing that a rattled, uncertain moment behind a senior leader's calm exterior is normal, not evidence of unique competence.
quotes: You have probably watched someone three levels up take in a situation you have been agonising over for two weeks and make the call in ninety seconds, and the only available explanation is that they know something you don't.

From the outside, watch the body: someone avoiding a decision goes still, sits back, stops gesturing and the voice flattens out, while someone actually wrestling with the problem leans in and gets more animated.
If the calendar is full of check-ins and nothing has been written, built or decided in between, you are just circling rather than deliberating.

Colette described being visibly rattled during an evening deployment that was not working, with a colleague pacing near her desk, and how saying "I don't know how we're going to do this" out loud made the situation worse for everyone.
So, remember: the people who look settled in the room have mostly just had longer to get used to the feeling.
